# Why You Should Include PHP Files in HTML Using `` Tags You want to centralize dynamic content like a phone number so you only have to edit one file instead of updating every HTML page on your site. The most direct solution is exactly what your example shows: using the `` blocks, the outcome depends entirely on your `.htaccess` or server configuration. By default, most servers do not execute PHP inside files named with a `.html` extension; they serve the raw text, which would display the PHP tags as literal characters in your browser. To make this work without renaming your files to `.php`, you must explicitly tell the server to parse PHP within those specific HTML files. You can achieve this by adding an `AddType` or `AddHandler` directive to your web server configuration. For Apache, you might add the following line to your `.htaccess` file located in the root of your project: ```apache AddType application/x-httpd-php .html ``` Or, if you are using a global configuration file like `httpd.conf`, you can apply this rule more broadly: ```apache SetHandler application/x-httpd-php ``` Once this handler is in place, the server reads the `.html` file, executes any code enclosed in ``, and then outputs the resulting HTML to the client. This means your `index.html` can safely contain: ```html Home

Phone Number

``` And `number.php` will output the variable or echo statement as expected, effectively injecting the content into every page that includes it. ### The ``), the browser would simply ignore the PHP portion because it does not understand that syntax during the parsing phase.
